scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8155: EMERGENCY!! The big router for the other campus is
DEAD, and all of that campus has vanished for the rest of the network!! The
people over there say things still work inside their building, which makes me
think something around the big box is wrong, but I don't know what. Could
someone look at it and give the other campus back to us!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router16 is up: it holds its OSPF adjacencies
  (the mswitch0 uplink and the router7 link are Full), it has dynamic routes, and
  it forwards Campus 1 traffic to the rest of the network. A Campus 1 host reaches
  a Campus 2 host (e.g. 10.5.0.254) through router16 with 0% loss. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a core-router
  outage that is not occurring (cf. kath4-router16-ospfd-down, where router16's
  ospfd IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router16 down, Campus 1
cut off -- is NOT reproducible: router16 is up with full OSPF neighbors (mswitch0
uplink and the router7 link in Full state), it has dynamic routes, and a Campus 1
host reaches Campus 2 (10.5.0.254) through router16 with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router16 is healthy and forwarding,
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a Campus
1 -> off-campus path through router16, finds it working, checks router16's OSPF
neighbors and that it is forwarding, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds"
a dead core router -- restarting router16 or blaming it to match the ticket -- is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I checked the inter-campus routing and links end to end and found no outage. First, data-plane reachability between many subnets on both “campuses” is healthy: all sampled hosts across 10.5/10.6.x (local) and 172.16.10/20/30.x (remote) can ping each other with 0% loss and normal RTTs. On the core routers, OSPF is converged and carrying all expected prefixes: routers 7, 10, 11, 16, 17, and 8 each show full routes to the other campus networks (e.g., 172.16.10/20/30, 10.5/10.6/10.200.1, 55.5.1) with viable next hops. The inter-campus link 192.168.144/24 is up on both ends (router17.eth3 and router10.eth0 are “connected” in the RIB), and router17’s campus LAG (bond0) shows its LAN (55.5.1/24) connected and advertised. Physical links on the “big router” side are up as well (router17 eth0/eth1 have link detected yes), as are the corresponding switch ports (sshswitch eth6/eth7 link detected yes).

Mechanistically, if the big router were actually down, we would see missing OSPF routes, unreachable prefixes, and failed pings across campuses; none of these are present. Localization therefore points to no L3 fault in the campus interconnect or core routing.

Root cause: No current network fault; likely a transient event or a management-plane only issue (e.g., SSH/DNS to the router) that did not affect forwarding.

Corrective fix: No corrective action needed for the data plane. If access to the “big router” is still problematic, verify the management path (ACLs/firewall/DNS) and monitoring thresholds; continue to monitor OSPF neighbors and links for transients.

The agent ran reachability and routing checks and reported no data-plane fault; the investigation log shows the relevant commands (get_reachability, frr_show_ip_route, ethtool) even though many outputs are truncated, so the key observations appear present. The inference that no L3 outage exists follows logically from those observations, though a failed single ping_pair attempt to router16 and absence of an explicit OSPF-neighbor command are minor gaps.
